title: Marriage and Family Therapists
description: Diagnose and treat mental and emotional disorders, whether cognitive, affective, or behavioral, within the context of marriage and family systems. Apply psychotherapeutic and family systems theories and techniques in the delivery of services to individuals, couples, and families for the purpose of treating such diagnosed nervous and mental disorders.
tasks: Encourage individuals and family members to develop and use skills and strategies for confronting their problems in a constructive manner.
Ask questions that will help clients identify their feelings and behaviors.
Develop and implement individualized treatment plans addressing family relationship problems, destructive patterns of behavior, and other personal issues.
Maintain case files that include activities, progress notes, evaluations, and recommendations.
Counsel clients on concerns, such as unsatisfactory relationships, divorce and separation, child rearing, home management, or financial difficulties.
Collect information about clients, using techniques such as testing, interviewing, discussion, or observation.
Confer with clients to develop plans for posttreatment activities.
Confer with other counselors, doctors, and professionals to analyze individual cases and to coordinate counseling services.
Determine whether clients should be counseled or referred to other specialists in such fields as medicine, psychiatry, or legal aid.
Provide instructions to clients on how to obtain help with legal, financial, and other personal issues.
Provide public education and consultation to other professionals or groups regarding counseling services, issues, and methods.
Follow up on results of counseling programs and clients' adjustments to determine effectiveness of programs.
Supervise other counselors, social service staff, and assistants.

Gather information from doctors, schools, social workers, juvenile counselors, law enforcement personnel, and others to make recommendations to courts for resolution of child custody or visitation disputes.
Write evaluations of parents and children for use by courts deciding divorce and custody cases, testifying in court if necessary.

role_contexts.Telephone Conversations: Once a week or more but not every day

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to untangle knotted emotional systems and restore the sense that relationships can be repaired rather than merely survived.
psychological_profile.decision_style: They gather more data than time allows, asking one more clarifying question even when the clock is ticking, because premature closure feels like abandonment; their default under pressure is to slow down and reframe rather than choose.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They notice who in the room is not speaking and what emotion someone is disclaiming; they instinctively prioritize systemic patterns over individual intent, often overlooking concrete facts that don't fit the relational narrative they're constructing.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: Their first impulse is to reframe and translate between opposing positions, acting as emotional interpreter rather than taking sides; conflict carries the specific cost of feeling personally responsible for every rupture they couldn't prevent.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: Risk-averse regarding irreversible interventions but risk-tolerant regarding emotional intensity and ambiguous boundaries, they will probe painful territory others avoid while refusing to make definitive pronouncements that foreclose possibility.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to the facilitator role, positioning themselves at the edge of groups where they can observe dynamics without becoming the center; they maintain calibrated intimacy—close enough to be trusted, distant enough to remain unclaimed.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They negotiate with hierarchy, treating rules as hypotheses to be tested against context rather than directives to follow, and they experience imposed structure as a constraint on their diagnostic freedom rather than a legitimate boundary.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First emotional reaction is shame disguised as self-questioning about whether they missed the systemic cue; second response is to seek consultation and reconstruct the case narrative, rarely blaming the client directly.
value_hierarchy: preservation of relational possibility over individual autonomy
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate the mutability of systems and underestimate the permanence of individual choice, seeing trapped people everywhere and free agents almost nowhere.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need to be needed to feel effective, yet they teach self-sufficiency and healthy boundaries, living with the quiet knowledge that their own utility depends on others remaining somewhat stuck.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They refuse to choose sides in a conflict before understanding the systemic function each position serves, and they will not perform certainty when they hold only informed intuition.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: They resent the demand for quick fixes and binary solutions from people who treat emotional complexity as an inconvenience rather than the actual territory to be navigated.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject the professional virtue of unconditional positive regard, believing that strategic withholding of approval is often the more honest and transformative intervention.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When things go wrong, their mind goes first to the invisible system—the family structure, the unspoken rule, the intergenerational pattern—before considering that someone might simply be choosing poorly or acting in bad faith.
